final.title: Focus blocks come after the workflow decision
final.body:
Before you protect a focus block, decide what is actually stealing the focus.

For a small business owner, the useful question is not whether AI sounds smart. It is whether one recurring task keeps interrupting the day: repeated customer questions, invoice data entry, or lead follow-up. If the same kind of work shows up again and again, you are looking at a workflow. If it changes every time, it is probably not the first thing to automate. That distinction matters more than the tool.

A simple check helps: does the task follow a pattern, repeat weekly, and have a clear input and output? If yes, it is worth measuring before you make room for automation. If no, keep it manual and move on. No spreadsheet heroics required; a plain week of notes is usually enough to tell whether you have a process or just a busy Tuesday.

That is the bounded decision Bareni starts with: identify one recurring workflow, say honestly whether AI fits, and then decide whether it should stay manual, be shared with a hire, or be scoped for a pilot. The normal sequence is a free 30-minute diagnostic, a free one-page pilot proposal, and then a paid working MVP in days or a fixed-price pilot in weeks. Those timings are intended scopes, not guarantees.

The first move is simple: name the one task, time how often it interrupts your week, and check whether it repeats in a pattern before you protect the block.

That is the kind of decision Bareni starts with.
